summary: Defines terms for benchmarking how quickly link-state routing protocols like IS-IS and OSPF settle on new routes after a change. The measurements are black-box and look only at data-plane behavior seen from outside. It is the vocabulary document for the methods in RFC 6413.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC is a vocabulary for one job: measuring how long a router takes to move traffic to a new path after something fails. It defines when a change counts as finished and gives three ways to turn packet counts into a convergence time. The test procedures themselves are in RFC 6413.

subtitle: The shared vocabulary for timing how fast a router settles on new paths, measured only from outside the router.

tldr.problem: Measuring how fast a link-state IGP such as IS-IS or OSPF moves traffic to a new path after a change only produces comparable numbers if every tester uses the same words and the same instants.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the convergence types, the named instants and transitions, the interfaces, three measurement methods and the resulting time benchmarks, all derived from data-plane traffic observed at a Tester.
tldr.outcome: It is the terminology companion to RFC 6413, which supplies the test methodology, and the metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6412 is a vocabulary document. It is the companion to RFC 6413, which contains the methodology for benchmarking link-state Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) route convergence, and it introduces the terms that methodology needs. The measurements are black-box: the tester watches the data plane through the Device Under Test (DUT) at the Tester and never inspects the router's internals.

The terms apply to IPv4 and IPv6 traffic and to link-state IGPs such as Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF). IGP convergence time is measured by observing the data plane through the DUT at the Tester.

The document reuses terminology from earlier IETF work, such as Throughput, Offered Load, Forwarding Rate and Forwarding Delay, and it uses the RFC 2119 requirement keywords even though it is not a Standards Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a word list for one job: measuring how long a router takes to move traffic to a new path after something fails. It defines when the move is finished and how to turn packet counts into a number. The test procedures are in RFC 6413.

sections.title: Route Convergence and Full Convergence
sections.content:
Route Convergence is the process of updating all components of the router, including the Routing Information Base (RIB) and the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) along with software and hardware tables, with the most recent route changes, such that forwarding for a route entry is successful on the Next-Best Egress Interface. Full Convergence is Route Convergence for all routes in the FIB.

In general, IGP convergence does not necessarily result in a change in forwarding. The test cases in RFC 6413 are specified so that convergence does change the egress interface for the measurement traffic. That property is what lets a tester observe Route Convergence and Full Convergence from outside the router, by seeing the measurement traffic rerouted to the Next-Best Egress Interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Two terms say how much of the router has caught up. Route convergence means one route has been updated everywhere inside the router and traffic to it now leaves by the new path. Full convergence means every route in the router has been updated that way.

sections.title: Instants, Transitions and Interfaces
sections.content:
The RFC names four instants in time. The Traffic Start Instant is the time the Tester sends out the first data packet to the DUT. The Convergence Event Instant is the time the event occurs. The First Route Convergence Instant is the time the first route entry completes Route Convergence. The Convergence Recovery Instant is the time Full Convergence has completed; that completed state must then be maintained for the Sustained Convergence Validation Time before the instant is valid.

Two transitions describe what the tester sees in between. The Convergence Event Transition is the interval after the event in which the Forwarding Rate on the Preferred Egress Interface gradually reduces to zero. The Convergence Recovery Transition is the interval after the First Route Convergence Instant in which the Forwarding Rate on the DUT egress interfaces gradually increases back to the Offered Load. Neither transition has to be linear, and the Offered Load, the number of routes and the Packet Sampling Interval all influence what is observed.

Four interface terms say where traffic leaves. A Local Interface is an interface on the DUT, and its failure means the failure happened directly on the DUT. A Remote Interface is an interface on a neighbouring router that is not directly connected to the DUT. The Preferred Egress Interface is the outbound interface for traffic routed to the preferred next hop, in other words the interface used before the event. The Next-Best Egress Interface is the outbound interface, or set of outbound interfaces in an Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) set or parallel link set, for traffic routed to the second-best next hop, in other words the interface used after the event.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives each moment of the change a name, so two testers record the same thing. It also names the router ports involved: the port traffic left by before the change, and the port it leaves by afterwards.

sections.title: Three Ways to Measure Convergence
sections.content:
The Rate-Derived Method computes benchmarks by observing the Forwarding Rate in every Packet Sampling Interval. At least one packet per route for all routes matched in the Offered Load must be offered to the DUT within each interval, and the interval should be as small as possible for maximum accuracy, although IP Packet Delay Variation (IPDV) may require a larger one. Because this method does not distinguish between individual traffic destinations, it should not be used for route-specific measurements, and in particular not for the Route Loss of Connectivity Period.

The Loss-Derived Method computes benchmarks from the number of Impaired Packets, which are packets that were lost, delayed beyond the Forwarding Delay Threshold, corrupted, duplicated or reordered. Since this method does not distinguish between traffic destinations and the impaired packet statistics are only collected after Full Convergence completion, it can only be used to measure average values over all routes, and therefore only the Loss-Derived Convergence Time and the Loss-Derived Loss of Connectivity Period.

The Route-Specific Loss-Derived Method gives each stream a single destination address matching a different route entry, and measures Convergence Packet Loss for each stream separately. The RFC marks it as the RECOMMENDED method for convergence time benchmarks, because it observes the impaired packet count the way a network user would experience it. Both loss-based methods should always be combined with the Rate-Derived Method, so that the completion of Full Convergence is observed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to time the change. One counts packets arriving in each short window. One counts the packets that were lost, too late, corrupted, duplicated or out of order. The third counts those bad packets separately for each destination. The RFC recommends the third, because it is the only one that says which routes were hit.

sections.title: The Benchmarks the Methods Produce
sections.content:
Full Convergence Time is the Convergence Recovery Instant minus the Convergence Event Instant, and First Route Convergence Time is the First Route Convergence Instant minus the Convergence Event Instant. Both come from the Rate-Derived Method, and neither can be measured with the Loss-Derived Method. For the test cases in RFC 6413, Full Convergence Time is expected to equal the maximum Route-Specific Convergence Time, and First Route Convergence Time the minimum.

Route-Specific Convergence Time is computed for one route as Connectivity Packet Loss divided by the Offered Load per route. When the event does not cause instantaneous traffic loss for all routes, the Convergence Packet Loss for that route is used instead and the interval between the Traffic Start Instant and the Convergence Event Instant is subtracted. The Loss-Derived Convergence Time is the same calculation averaged over all routes. The per-route results can be reported as a minimum, maximum, average and median.

The Route Loss of Connectivity Period is how long packets to one route were impaired after the event until Full Convergence completed. It is smaller than the Route-Specific Convergence Time when the router keeps forwarding traffic on the Preferred Egress Interface for a while, which is the case after a failure is reversed. The two are equal only when traffic for all routes starts dropping instantaneously at the Convergence Event Instant. The Loss-Derived Loss of Connectivity Period is the average of that period over all routes.

Two measurement settings shape every result. The Packet Sampling Interval is the interval at which the Tester polls for arriving packets; it should be as small as possible, but a small interval makes the Forwarding Rate fluctuate when IPDV is present, and an interval longer than the convergence itself hides the instants. The Sustained Convergence Validation Time is how long the completed state must hold without further impaired packets; the RECOMMENDED value is the time to send 5 consecutive packets to each destination with a minimum of 5 seconds, chosen from RFC 2544, which recommends waiting 2 seconds for residual frames to arrive and 5 seconds for the DUT to restabilise. The Forwarding Delay Threshold separates packets that are merely very late from packets that will never arrive; it is a parameter of the methodology and must be reported, and RFC 2544 recommends 2 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The scores are simple differences between named moments, and the loss-based scores are bad-packet counts divided by the traffic rate. Two settings decide how accurate the numbers are: how often the tester counts packets, and how long the router must hold still before the change counts as finished. Both are stated in the RFC, so two laboratories get comparable results.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking activities as described in this memo are limited to technology characterization using controlled stimuli in a laboratory environment, with dedicated address space. The benchmarking network topology must be an independent test setup and must not be connected to devices that may forward the test traffic into a production network or misroute traffic to the test management network.

Benchmarking is performed on a black-box basis, relying solely on measurements observable external to the DUT or SUT. Special capabilities should not exist in the DUT or SUT specifically for benchmarking purposes, so any security implications arising from the device should be identical in the lab and in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the tests on a separate network with its own address space, and do not connect that network to production equipment. Measure only what an outside observer can see, and do not add benchmarking-only features to the router.

data.title: Convergence time calculations
data.code:
Full Convergence Time =
    Convergence Recovery Instant - Convergence Event Instant

  Connectivity Packet Loss for specific route / Offered Load per route
